title: Rahul Gandhi: India bloc leaders march to Supreme Court as protests continue
description: India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.  This
body: India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.  This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital.Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained.Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge.The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons".He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter."Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters.Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march.In a press conference on Monday, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to the Chief Justice, laying out their concerns with Kumar's alleged conduct and with the contentious electoral roll revision.He said that Kant had asked them to file a petition, which they would do at the end of their march.Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march.Several thousand people were on Barakhamba road, where the march began, as a bus carrying Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders arrived just before 15:30 local time. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind Rahul was Neha Bora, a leftist student leader who has gained prominence for participating in the protests.Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists."Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

schema.headline: Rahul Gandhi: India bloc leaders march to Supreme Court as protests continue

title: Golf: DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season
description: Players who sign up to LIV Golf next season will not be allowed to be members of the European Tour in 2027.The European Tour, which is sponsored by DP
body: Players who sign up to LIV Golf next season will not be allowed to be members of the European Tour in 2027.The European Tour, which is sponsored by DP World, said players must "make a choice" regarding where they play - a significantly tougher stance than in recent seasons.Only players who are members of the DP World Tour can play for Europe in the Ryder Cup.Deadlines for both tours are in the next five weeks, though there remains uncertainty surrounding LIV Golf's future despite it securing a possible $300m in funding as it attempts to restructure."Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, CEO of the DP World Tour, told BBC Sport."We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by."Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV.However, players will be asked to disclose which tours they intend to play on for next year, and their answer will be taken into account when deciding on their membership.While the DP World Tour agreed to grant conditional releases with nine players this season, it is understood the change for 2027 is predominantly down to LIV offering players equity in future and a feeling this is incompatible with the European tour being a members organisation.However, it also comes at a time when the DP World Tour's strategic alliance with the PGA Tour is being negotiated, so the move likely reflects a desire to put itself in the best position possible in those discussions.Players will have until 16 November to sign up to the DP World Tour for next year.Under the terms of its court-supervised restructuring process, LIV Golf needs to sign players up by 25 October.Ted Goldthorpe, head of BC Partners Credit, told BBC Sport last week he was "confident" LIV would have a "critical mass" of players.But since then two-time major winner Rahm has said he will not continue playing on the LIV tour.Lawyers representing a number of other players, including fellow major winners Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith, sought clarification from the court that rejection of contracts would equate to "termination", enabling players to hold discussions with third parties about their futures.Richard Bland is currently the only player to have stated publicly a desire to play on LIV 2.0.However, Perez indicated last month he hoped there would be a future for the league.

schema.headline: Golf: DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season

title: Burnham says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit referendum
description: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The
body: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was.""I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.Asked about the prime minister's comments on BBC Breakfast, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty said he wouldn't "get into specifics" of Russian interference in the 2016 vote when pushed for evidence."Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes," Doughty told the BBC. "They're engaged in information warfare, they're spending £1.5bn this year alone on disinformation and propaganda." Doughty also denied that Burnham was raising the issue of Russian interference in the Brexit referendum because he wants to rejoin the EU. He said: "This is a broader point he is making about Russian attempts to destabilise and interfere in our democracy."Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016". It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016. "It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week."There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics. In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums.It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat.In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia".And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections.In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election.BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine. One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price.Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world"."There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added. Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears".He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation. A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values."We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies."

schema.headline: Burnham says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit referendum

title: NFL: San Francisco 49ers & Minnesota Vikings go 5-0
description: San Francisco beat Super Bowl champions Seattle 32-29 in a typically brutal contest between divisional rivals, with the Niners having defensive star D
body: San Francisco beat Super Bowl champions Seattle 32-29 in a typically brutal contest between divisional rivals, with the Niners having defensive star Dre Greenlaw ejected early on for a headbutt on Ernest Jones, who was not wearing a helmet, on the sidelines.Both defences are elite and forced a season-high seven turnovers in the game, with the 49ers in particular taking advantage by scoring three touchdowns from theirs. The 21 points off turnovers was the most Seattle have allowed in a decade.Brock Purdy eventually got San Francisco over the line thanks to new wide receiver Mike Evans, who had 113 yards receiving and a touchdown, taking some great catches late on.The only team to have a top-five scoring offence and defence, the 49ers again have injury problems this season, but if Evans stays fit he could be the missing piece in the puzzle.San Francisco are now 5-0 for the third time under head coach Kyle Shanahan. They made the Super Bowl on both previous occasions and, if they keep finding ways to win, they have every chance again.The Minnesota Vikings are also 5-0 after another defensive masterclass from Brian Flores' unit in their 23-13 win at the slumping New Orleans Saints.With wins over the Saints (1-4), Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) and Miami Dolphins (0-5), we will know more about the Vikings after their bye, but allowing only 13 points a game will always give you a chance.There was a comedy of errors at the end of the Washington Commanders' 27-27 tie with the New York Giants as both teams fluffed their lines with victory within their grasp.The Giants scored two late touchdowns to force overtime but, when within range of a winning field goal, they ran the ball with Cam Skattebo, who fumbled to lose possession.Washington then had the game at their mercy in the dying seconds but, instead of taking the kick, ran a play - and ran out of time.With play-calling like that, neither team deserved to win.The Baltimore Ravens showed them both how it is done as quarterback Lamar Jackson's back-up Tyler Huntley earned a 30-23 overtime victory at the Atlanta Falcons, throwing a touchdown with 40 seconds left of regulation time before running in the game-winner in the extra period.The Ravens are 4-1 and lurking.More poor finishing came in the rain in New York as the Cleveland Browns missed an extra point and then Corey Bojorquez fumbled a late punt which the Jets turned into the winning touchdown.Although it was messy at times, the Jets seem to have a fine defence, with eight sacks on Deshaun Watson in their 17-12 success.

schema.headline: NFL: San Francisco 49ers & Minnesota Vikings go 5-0

title: How to avoid getting stung with bad debt advice if you miss a credit card payment
description: The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice chariti
body: The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for.A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities.Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says.Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond.Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first.And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details."Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange.

schema.headline: How to avoid getting stung with bad debt advice if you miss a credit card payment

title: Australia v South Africa: Bad light thwarts Durban Test despite ICC changes
description: Play is already starting at 09:30 local time in Durban. This is the first October Test at Kingsmead, where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this ti
body: Play is already starting at 09:30 local time in Durban. This is the first October Test at Kingsmead, where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this time of year on South Africa's eastern coast.Still, on day one, play was halted at 15:23 local time after clouds built. Only 65.2 of the scheduled 90 overs had been bowled and the players were unable to return.Day two was slightly better with play continuing until 16:25, but that finish was still 35 minutes earlier than it could have been. Day three's end came at 16:31.On each occasion, the first two sessions have been played in hot, sunny conditions, only for clouds to build in the afternoon - a familiar weather pattern in Durban."Very quickly in the morning, as temperatures have risen inland as the sun heats the ground, a sea breeze has formed with winds coming from the sea into Durban," said BBC weather presenter Chris Fawkes."This has increased humidity levels through the morning and brought some cloud in. As temperatures have started to fall again towards the evening, this has increased the relative humidity with the air getting increasingly saturated."That has caused the cloud to get thicker and lower."One narrative exists that the pink ball moves more under floodlights, though that is not backed up by ball tracking data.Instead, various batters have spoken about the pink ball being more difficult to see. Batting averages are lowest in the evening of day-night matches.Australia have also played in 15 of Test cricket's day-nighters - 10 more than anyone else.Unsurprisingly, the four leading wicket-takers in day-night matches are all Australians. Left-armer Mitchell Starc's haul of 89 wickets in 15 Tests has positioned him as the undisputed pink-ball king.You would not blame teams if they would rather face Australia with the red ball.Former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander said he prefers the idea of switching balls during the match if conditions require it, but that would raise questions over the Test's integrity.Is the potential injustice of one team having to face a pink ball outweighed by the need to get more action of the field?"They have to take it out of the hands of the players completely and enforce it from the umpires' point of view that the pink ball will become in play when the light has faded enough," Philander said."You are always going to have the argument of who is ahead of the game."I would like to see the ICC enforce it on to the officials to make that call."

schema.headline: Australia v South Africa: Bad light thwarts Durban Test despite ICC changes

title: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds
description: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.Accounts s
body: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree". MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

schema.headline: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds

title: Kenyan mourners killed by police at Raila Odinga memorial not involved in violence, BBC Africa Eye finds
description: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that s
body: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute."The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons. The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection. The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.

schema.headline: Kenyan mourners killed by police at Raila Odinga memorial not involved in violence, BBC Africa Eye finds

title: Will Lankshear: The 'Kane-esque' striker Spurs may regret letting go
description: Leaping high, six yards out, to nod in Tommy Conway's cross from the left wing, Will Lankshear notched his ninth goal in 12 games for Middlesbrough.It
body: Leaping high, six yards out, to nod in Tommy Conway's cross from the left wing, Will Lankshear notched his ninth goal in 12 games for Middlesbrough.It is that positioning, finishing and poacher's instinct, earning Boro a 1-0 win against Wolves on Saturday, that has made Lankshear an instant hit at Riverside Stadium – and a cause of lament at Tottenham Hotspur.Lankshear joined Boro from Spurs in the summer on a five-year contract in a deal that could rise to a club record buy of £20m.Since then, he has scored as many goals in all competitions as Spurs' combined team. His old side, despite snatching a draw at Manchester United a few hours after Lankshear's latest winner, remain in the Premier League relegation zone while Boro sit in the Championship's automatic promotion places.Dominic Solanke's last-minute goal at Old Trafford was the first league goal scored by a Tottenham forward in five months.It is enough to make Spurs fans despair."A lot of fans are wondering why he was sold," Ali Speechly, co-chair of the Women of the Lane supporters' group, told BBC Sport."It was likely to do with money - his sell-on price is relatively high, so let's cash in on him."I was definitely disappointed. Given how badly we have started this season, as a fan it feels like the wrong decision."Amid a multi-million pound summer splurge, Spurs allowed Lankshear to leave for an initial fee worth about £10m, with an additional £10m due in add-ons based on various clauses.Boro saw off competition around the Championship, and in Europe, to sign the 21-year-old who impressed at Oxford United in the second tier last season, scoring 12 league goals on loan for a relegated side.Good form for a young player, but not so compelling he had to go straight into the Spurs first team."If you are a young kid at a club where you are not getting any first-team football and you get the opportunity to go and play men's football, you should go," former Spurs goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Sport."The academies are great and Premier League 2 is a great feeder for the first team, but if you are 21, 22 or 23 and still mostly playing in the under-23s then you have missed the boat."Getting first-team football is the best grounding you can get for a young footballer, getting the opportunity to play in the first team, regardless of what league it is. Will has been given this opportunity, and he is taking it."Lankshear scored 23 goals for Tottenham's U23 team in the 2023–24 Premier League 2 season and played for the senior side in the 2024-25 Europa League campaign – most notably scoring then getting sent off against Galatasaray.But amid a churn of players and managers at Spurs, he has moved on – and Boro fans couldn't be happier.Middlesbrough have built a reputation in recent years of providing a springboard for promising youngsters. Most notably, Morgan Rogers spent six months at Riverside Stadium before joining Aston Villa, and the rest is history.Not only that, but Boro - who missed out on promotion last season after scoring only once in three play-off games - badly needed a skilful, physical presence who could finish the multitude of chances made by Kim Hellberg's creative but blunt side."Boro was a team that made a boatload of chances, and he knew he would be able to get on the end of them," BBC Tees commentator Mark Drury told BBC Sport."But what people have been impressed with is his instinctive finishing - one touch, just being in the right place. It's simple but not a lot of people know how to be there at the right time, to give yourself the highest percentage chance."He's taller and stockier than he might look from the sidelines, and he is only 21. He seems to have the all-round package - good with both feet and in the air."A 6ft 2in English striker with a deadly finishing touch, who came through at Spurs before learning his trade in the Football League. Remind you of anyone?"I can understand the comparisons with Harry Kane," said Robinson. "He has headed down a similar career path to Harry and, physically, he has a similar stature as well."Like Kane, he looks like a player who is developing a little later, compared to others who are Premier League regulars before the end of their teens."You look at him and the career path he is on; it is a very similar one to the one Harry Kane has been on, and that is a big positive. There is no substitute for playing in the first team somewhere, regardless of what level you are playing at."Like Kane, Lankshear also had early career setbacks. Initially at Arsenal's academy, he was released and signed with Sheffield United before being picked up by Spurs for £2m when he was 17.He also had hit-and-miss loan spells. An unremarkable stint at West Brom was followed by a more fruitful spell with Oxford."Harry Kane didn't always have brilliantly successful loan spells, they are not always a marker of a player," says Speechly."He didn't do anything remarkable, but it is unfortunate as we are not scoring goals. It is painful to see."I don't think we will ever get another Kane, but there are definitely similarities. He is a real poacher and has a strong work ethic. It is very Kane-esque."Tottenham do not have the right to immediately bring Lankshear back next summer. Clauses in the deal give them the right to be notified of and match any future accepted bid that Middlesbrough receive, and Spurs will get 20% of any profit on any future sale.They have first refusal rather than a guaranteed, pre-set buy-back, but there remains a feeling Boro are enjoying Lankshear while they can."It's just the reality of life, definitely in the Championship but certainly in the Premier League," said Drury. "There is always a pecking order."Lankshear seems to have all the tools, including attitude, to make the best of the talent he has got. If he continues at this rate of progress, it would be no surprise to see him in the Premier League - hopefully with the Boro."Such has been Lankshear's form, there has even been talk of a step up from the England under-21s, for who he scored on his debut last month.Referencing potential punishments for Manchester City, England manager Thomas Tuchel said he was open to calling up players outside the Premier League, external.If he is succession planning for 33-year-old Kane, given a paucity of top-flight options, a Lankshear call-up may not be so far-fetched.

schema.headline: Will Lankshear: The 'Kane-esque' striker Spurs may regret letting go

title: AI cameras spot nearly 19,000 road offences in West Midlands
description: An artificial intelligence trial identified almost 19,000 potential driving offences in Birmingham and Wolverhampton in just two weeks.West Midlands m
body: An artificial intelligence trial identified almost 19,000 potential driving offences in Birmingham and Wolverhampton in just two weeks.West Midlands mayor Richard Parker called the findings "shocking" saying the number of drivers putting themselves and others at risk was "far higher than we expected".The trial used AI-powered cameras outside Ladywood and Fallings Park fire stations in March to identify potential seatbelt and mobile phone offences.The images they captured included a front-seat passenger holding a small child on their lap without a seatbelt and a driver holding a mobile phone with both hands.Dozens of images showed children travelling without age-appropriate restraints.At Ladywood, the technology identified 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences. At Fallings Park, it recorded 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences.Parker said: "The number of people risking their own lives and the lives of others, including some very young children, is frankly shocking and far higher than we expected."I've met families who have lost loved ones to reckless driving," he added. "They never recover from those tragedies."He said he would use "every resource available" to make roads safer as the findings were reviewed. The trial was funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority working with the police and fire service. No enforcement is planned as a result of the trial, which was intended to establish the potential scale of mobile phone use and failures to use child restraints.Simon Foster, West Midlands police and crime commissioner and chairman of the region's road safety partnership board, said the findings were "deeply concerning". "We are closely evaluating these trial results to consider how this advanced AI technology can be deployed for future police enforcement," he added. "We will use every effective tool at our disposal to ensure our roads are safer."Mat MacDonald, the West Midlands road safety commissioner, said mobile phone use at the wheel and failing to wear a seatbelt were two of the leading causes of death and serious injury on the region's roads.The WMCA said road safety data for last year showed mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths on UK roads while unfastened seatbelts were linked to 133 deaths.About 2,000 drivers a year in the West Midlands are fined and given penalty points for using a phone while driving.

schema.headline: AI cameras spot nearly 19,000 road offences in West Midlands

title: Women's football: Billion-dollar boom is leaving players behind - Fifpro raises concerns
description: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure cont
body: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress.That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro., externalPlayers were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46%. Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors."Players are now very visible," she said."Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive."While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone."Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said.In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs.One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status.Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing.In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur.All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club.However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football."Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said.The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (£1,250).Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (£363) in Africa.While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage.Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels.Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries.Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income."Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin."There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year."She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities.Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere.Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis".The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension.Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality."I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said.However, not all trends were negative.One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood.In 2017, nearly half of respondents considering leaving the game early said wanting a family could drive them out of football.That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago."What we've concluded, which I think is incredibly important, is that targeted regulatory intervention works - maternity regulations were introduced in 2021," said Culvin.The report highlights a widening divide within the women's game. The sport's elite clubs and players have benefited from investment and visibility, yet much of the global workforce remains vulnerable."You've got an industry that's very focused on the top 5% of players," Culvin said."But then what you've got is the rest, which is 95% of the industry who are not paid on time, who have short contracts. They don't get paid for 12 months - they are in incredibly vulnerable and precarious environments."Despite that, Fifpro insists the solution is not to slow down growth but to ensure that commercial success and player welfare develop together."There doesn't need to be a choice for those between commercial growth and player protection," said Culvin."Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem."Her conclusion is clear."What we're saying is enough is enough and the industry needs to react to the players' needs and centralise the players' voice, ensure that players have a seat at the table when decisions that affect them are being made about them."

schema.headline: Women's football: Billion-dollar boom is leaving players behind - Fifpro raises concerns

title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
description: Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not nec
body: Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice.The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them.It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket.The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters.She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of £5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete."We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said.Her neighbour's house was also damaged. "They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC.The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly."In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing. Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before.Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them."Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said.Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics.Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England.Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for £250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost £2,500."An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said.It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500," she said.But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said.To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests:Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callersGather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receiptsKnow your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refundLord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes".He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes."Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said.

schema.headline: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds

title: Sinn Féin ministers facing no-confidence vote after Drumcree dispute
description: The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.Jim Allister has been urging
body: The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister.The DUP leader Gavin Robinson told Good Morning Ulster: "When somebody breaks the law they should be punished for breaking the law."He said that removing Little-Pengelly would "punish everybody else"."Colleagues and I have discussed continually about options that are available to us."It is absurd that there will be a motion of no confidence, which we know before it starts, whether it concludes successfully, we know it can't because of the system that we have."Robinson added that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise".However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position.Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position".He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents".DUP MP Gregory Campbell said his party would not be collapsing Stormont, but that he does believe that now is a time for "very stringent action"."We have got to take some action now to ensure that the law is upheld," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme."But we're not going to commit grievous bodily harm by walking out of Stormont."Campbell said his party colleague Carla Lockhart is "absolutely right"  when she says it cannot be business as usual at Stormont.He said his view is that is if a minister has been "convicted in a court of law of a criminal offence, a serious criminal offence, there has to be a sanction that would prevent that person from holding office."The DUP, he added, had the support of its members in relation to the approach it is taking."We've taken soundings throughout the party and people are confident in what we've been doing."They are looking for action, they're going to get action."

title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
description: Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after
body: Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

schema.headline: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports

title: Man denies racist murder of scientist in Dundee
description: A man has denied the racially-aggravated murder of a scientist on a Dundee street.Kyler Rattray, 21, is accused of attacking Dr Fortune Gomo in South
body: A man has denied the racially-aggravated murder of a scientist on a Dundee street.Kyler Rattray, 21, is accused of attacking Dr Fortune Gomo in South Street in July last year.Prosecutors allege the 39-year-old academic was repeatedly struck on the body with a knife and that the attack was aggravated by prejudice relating to race, colour nationality or ethnicity.The trial is due to begin on 5 January 2028 at the High Court in Dundee and is expected to last eight days.Rattray also faces a separate charge of illegally having a knife in a public place.The case called at a virtual hearing at the High Court in Glasgow earlier.Dr Gomo was found fatally injured on the street and was treated by paramedics at the scene, but never recovered.At the time, Police Scotland acknowledged that her death had caused great shock throughout Dundee.She was originally from Mutare in eastern Zimbabwe, had graduated with a PhD from Dundee University, and had recently started working for Scottish Water.

schema.headline: Man denies racist murder of scientist in Dundee
